findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage... (Maricopa §8.2.10) // Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000 (Sacramento §III.A)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Pg 6 of 41 §8.2.10; Sacramento Pg 2 of 4 §III.A
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No General Liability policy submitted in this program review. Only Commercial Auto (Hanover AW4-H221414-05, eff 4/1/25–4/1/26) was provided.
findings.gap_description: No General Liability policy was provided as part of the program submission. Both Maricopa County (Arizona) and Sacramento County (California) require Commercial General Liability with specific limits ($2M/$4M/$4M and $1M/$2M respectively), additional insured status, primary & noncontributory wording, waiver of subrogation, contractual liability, and blanket/broad terms. Without a CGL, every premises, products/completed operations, and personal/advertising injury claim arising from Run-Test's operations is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy is the only liability policy I was given. If a county employee, a poll worker, or a member of the public is injured at one of your facilities, slipped on a misprinted ballot box, or was hurt by a defectively printed ballot, there is currently no policy in this program to respond. Both Maricopa and Sacramento County contracts treat absence of GL as a material breach — and absent any policy at all, claims for bodily injury, property damage, and personal/advertising injury have no carrier to pay them. This is the largest uninsured exposure in your program.
findings.recommendation: Place a Commercial General Liability policy immediately. Minimum: $2M occurrence / $4M aggregate / $4M products-completed operations to satisfy Maricopa's higher threshold (which automatically satisfies Sacramento). Insist on ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form, blanket additional insured (CG 20 33 + CG 20 37 for ongoing AND completed operations using 'arising out of' language), blanket waiver of subrogation (CG 24 04), primary & noncontributory (CG 20 01), per-project aggregate (CG 25 03), unintentional E&O giveback, and a Notice/Knowledge of Occurrence endorsement limiting imputation of knowledge to officers. No XCU exclusion. No third-party action-over limitation. Until bound, do not begin or continue contract performance — both contracts treat lapse as material breach.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what happens if a county Risk Manager asks for your COI tomorrow — what GL document do you currently provide them?
When was the last time someone independently confirmed your GL policy was actually issued, in force, and matches contract specs — the carrier, broker, or just the certificate-issuing system?
If a poll worker tripped over election equipment your team delivered and broke a hip, who would you call first — and which insurance carrier would they ultimately bill?
How are you currently funding the indemnification obligations you've signed in your county contracts? If GL isn't in place, indemnity flows straight to the balance sheet.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability
findings.contract_quote: Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes... and Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit. (Maricopa §8.2.12) // WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. (Sacramento §III.C–D)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Pg 6 of 41 §8.2.12; Sacramento Pg 1–2 of 4 §II.C, §III.C–D
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Workers' Compensation policy submitted. Run-Test has 50–200 employees and operates in AZ and 30 other states.
findings.gap_description: No WC policy was provided. Arizona requires statutory workers' compensation for all employees. Sacramento requires CA-statutory WC plus EL $1M/accident/disease. Maricopa requires statutory WC plus EL $1M/$1M/$1M and waiver of subrogation. Without WC, the company faces uninsured employee injury claims, statutory penalties under A.R.S. §23-907, employer's liability tort exposure, and immediate breach of both contracts.
findings.plain_english: If a single employee is injured on the job today, the company pays out-of-pocket for medical, lost wages, and any tort claim — and Arizona can fine the company and pierce corporate protections for unpaid WC. With 50–200 employees, even one back injury or repetitive-stress claim can run into six figures. Both county contracts also flag WC as a strict-liability requirement; you can't begin work without it.
findings.recommendation: Place a Workers' Compensation policy with statutory coverage in AZ as the home state and Other States coverage (3.C) for every state where Run-Test has any employee presence — local, county, or state election work. Ensure California is on Item 3.A (not just 3.C) given the active Sacramento contract. EL limits at $1M/$1M/$1M to support umbrella attachment. Endorse Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (WC 04 03 for AZ; WC 04 03 06 for CA) and Notice of Cancellation to designated entities. Until bound, do not have any employee perform work in CA or under a Maricopa task order.
discoveryQuestions: When was your last Workers' Comp renewal, and who is the carrier? If you have one, why wasn't it included in this audit submission?
How are you currently handling claims when an employee gets hurt — you have 50 to 200 people, this happens?
When you send a print operator to a Sacramento County facility for installation, who's covering them under California WC — your AZ policy with Other States, or are you carrying a CA-specific policy?
Has anyone walked you through the personal-liability and corporate-veil exposure Arizona Industrial Commission can pursue if WC lapses? It's not just a fine.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Cyber / Network Security & Privacy Liability
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees... losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber Liability policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County requires a $5M Cyber/Network Security/Privacy Liability policy with one of the broadest enumerated coverage lists I've seen in a county contract: regulatory fines and penalties (not just defense), cyber extortion, network business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, and crisis management. No cyber policy was provided. Run-Test's core operations — election technology, ballot processing, voter data, election mail sorting — are exactly the operations cyber risk specialists target. The DHS designates election infrastructure as critical infrastructure (16th sector), and the Russian/Chinese threat actor activity around U.S. elections is well-documented. A breach affecting 90 million registered voters' data would be company-ending.
findings.plain_english: You handle data for 90+ million voters across 31 states. A ransomware event, a phishing-driven wire fraud, or a database breach would trigger 50 different state notification statutes, FBI involvement, regulatory investigations, and class-action litigation — all uninsured. Maricopa County contractually requires $5M of cyber coverage covering exactly this scenario, and the policy isn't there. This is the single most likely catastrophic exposure for an election services company, and there's currently no carrier to call.
findings.recommendation: Place standalone cyber liability coverage at $5M minimum (consider higher given voter-data exposure and critical-infrastructure designation). Insist on: 1st-party network business interruption with at least 8-hour waiting period, ransomware/extortion (preferably no sublimit or $2M+), social engineering (with reasonable sublimit), regulatory fines & penalties (where insurable by law), funds transfer fraud, computer fraud, system failure, dependent business interruption, breach response costs (notification, credit monitoring, forensics, crisis PR), retroactive date on or before Maricopa contract effective date, prior acts coverage, and reasonable retention. Use a specialty cyber market (Beazley, Coalition, Chubb, At-Bay, Resilience) — not a packaged sublimited cyber endorsement.
discoveryQuestions: Election infrastructure is federally designated critical infrastructure — when was your last tabletop exercise on what happens if your systems are encrypted on a Sunday night before a Tuesday election?
If your accounts payable team gets a spoofed email impersonating a county client and wires $200K, what policy responds today?
You serve over 90 million registered voters across 31 states — can you walk me through your incident response plan and where insurance would slot in?
Has Maricopa or any other county audited your COI for cyber compliance recently? They've been escalating cyber-spec scrutiny since 2024.

findings.contract_quote: If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements. (Maricopa §8.2.9) // UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) (Sacramento §II.E)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Pg 6 of 41 §8.2.9; Sacramento Pg 2 of 4 §II.E
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella or Excess Liability policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: No umbrella was provided. Both contracts contemplate umbrella stacking to reach minimum limits (Maricopa explicitly for CGL §8.2.10, Sacramento for GL/Auto/EL). Maricopa's $2M Auto CSL minimum cannot be reached on the current $1M Auto unless an umbrella sits over it. Beyond contract compliance, an election services company with PE backing, multi-state operations, fleet exposure, and high-stakes counterparties (counties, states, voter populations) carries catastrophic verdict potential — a single multi-vehicle accident, a ballot-error class action, or a defamation-style election claim can pierce primary limits.
findings.plain_english: Even if all your underlying policies were in place, you'd still be exposed for any claim that exceeds primary limits — and election services lawsuits are exactly the kind that go big. An umbrella is the cheapest insurance you can buy per dollar of limit, and Maricopa and Sacramento both expect one to be there. Without it, you're betting the company on every claim staying under $1M to $2M, which is not how plaintiff's lawyers operate.
findings.recommendation: Place a $5M–$10M Commercial Umbrella attaching over GL ($2M/$4M), Auto ($1M or $2M CSL), and EL ($1M/$1M/$1M). Confirm follow-form, no special exclusions broader than underlying, drop-down for reduced/exhausted aggregates, defense outside limits, blanket AI follow-form, blanket waiver of subrogation follow-form, per-project aggregate follow-form, no cyber exclusion, and that all underlying policies are correctly listed in the schedule. Confirm punitive damages NOT excluded (state law permitting). Consider $10M minimum given PE backing and $5M cyber underlying.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest jury verdict you've seen in your industry — and have you stress-tested that number against your current primary limits?
Your PE sponsor — are they aware that the program currently has no umbrella sitting above primary?
If a Run-Test van rear-ends a school bus, $1M Auto CSL is gone before the ambulances clear the scene. Walk me through what happens next.
Have you ever been pressured by a county to raise limits mid-contract? Both your Maricopa and Sacramento clauses reserve the right — what's your plan if that happens?

findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... Umbrella expressly cannot be used to satisfy this minimum (Section II.E).
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County requires standalone Professional Liability at $1M/$1M, with retro on or before contract effective date and 1-year ERP if claims-made cancelled or non-renewed. Umbrella cannot satisfy. No E&O policy was provided. Run-Test's services — ballot design, printing, mailing, sorting, election emergency support technology — create classic professional/E&O exposures: errors in ballot layout, mailing wrong materials to wrong voters, missed certification deadlines, faulty election technology integration. GL won't respond to economic/financial loss without bodily injury or property damage; cyber won't respond to professional negligence in services; these claims live and die on E&O.
findings.plain_english: If you misprint ballots, mail to the wrong precinct, or your election support technology fails on Election Day and a county sues for damages, that's an E&O claim — not a slip-and-fall. There's no policy in your current program that responds to professional negligence in election services. With your client list (counties, states, 90 million voters), the political and reputational stakes amplify any error, and one missed certification can end multi-year contracts. Sacramento contractually requires this — a COI without it is a non-starter.
findings.recommendation: Place a Professional Liability / E&O policy specifically scoped for election services / printing / data processing. Ensure: definition of 'Professional Services' explicitly captures ballot printing, mailing, election mail sorting, election support technology, voter data processing, and any consulting work; retro date on or before earliest active contract; full prior acts; broad consent-to-settle (avoid 80/20 hammer); $1M minimum (consider $2M–$5M given PE-backed scale); duty-to-defend; reasonable retention. Confirm the form does NOT exclude government contracts or election work specifically.
discoveryQuestions: If a county sues you because mail-in ballots arrived in the wrong envelopes the week before an election, which policy handles that — and what's the playbook?

You serve 31 states — how do you handle scope creep in services? Election technology consulting tends to slide from 'we deliver hardware' to 'we run the process.' What does that do to your professional exposure?
Has any client ever raised a contract claim against you for a printing or mailing error? How was it resolved, and was insurance involved?
Sacramento explicitly forbids using umbrella to satisfy E&O — were you aware of that, and how does your current program plan to comply?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Crime / Fidelity (Including Social Engineering)
findings.contract_quote: (Cyber spec)... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No Crime / Commercial Fidelity policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's cyber spec demands 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction.' These are classic Crime/Fidelity coverages — typically NOT robustly covered by standalone Cyber forms (Cyber tends to sublimit social engineering and computer crime to $250K–$500K). With no Cyber AND no Crime policy in the program, employee theft, vendor invoice fraud, social engineering wire transfers, ACH fraud, and forgery have nowhere to go. Run-Test handles county funds and processes large mailing volumes — both prime targets.
findings.plain_english: Two of the most common loss types for a company your size — an employee embezzling, or a finance person tricked into wiring money to a fake vendor — currently have no insurance backstop. Cyber forms partially address it but are typically too sublimited to matter. A real Crime policy with a Social Engineering / Fraudulent Instruction endorsement is what's needed. The contract's reference to 'third-party fidelity' specifically anticipates this.
findings.recommendation: Place a Commercial Crime / Fidelity policy with: Employee Theft ($1M+), Forgery or Alteration, Computer Fraud, Funds Transfer Fraud, Money Orders & Counterfeit Currency, AND a Social Engineering / Fraudulent Instruction endorsement at $250K–$500K minimum. Add Client Coverage (third-party fidelity) endorsement to satisfy Maricopa's third-party fidelity requirement. Ensure NO arrest/conviction prerequisite. Consider blanket vs. scheduled employee coverage (blanket strongly preferred).
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your dual-control process for outgoing wire transfers — and what would happen if it failed once?
How many people in your AP/finance group can issue payments? When was the last fraud-awareness training?
If an employee is embezzling from county funds you're processing, who pays the county back — you, or insurance?
Maricopa specifically called out 'third-party fidelity' in the cyber spec — that's actually a Crime coverage. Were you aware they were anticipating both?

findings.contract_quote: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: No Property or Inland Marine policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's client profile flags 'High-value equipment' as a risk. Election technology, printing presses, sorting machines, and scanners constitute significant fixed-asset exposure. Mobile/in-transit ballots, equipment delivered to county sites, and laptops/peripherals at temporary election locations are classic Inland Marine/Motor Truck Cargo exposures. Auto Liability EXCLUDES property in care/custody/control (CA 00 01 §II.B.6, Pg 34 of policy). Without Property and Inland Marine, fire/wind/theft at the AZ facility OR theft/damage of equipment in transit to a county is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Your business runs on expensive equipment — both at your AZ facility and on the road to client counties. If your printing press catches fire, or a truck of voting machines is stolen, neither your Auto policy nor any other policy in the program will pay. Sacramento's contract specifically anticipates Inland Marine and requires a waiver of subrogation if you have it — implying they expect you to have it.
findings.recommendation: Place a Property policy covering all owned/leased real and personal property at scheduled locations, with replacement cost, business income with extended period of indemnity (essential for election cycle revenue), equipment breakdown, and ordinance/law. Place Inland Marine covering: Contractors Equipment (the high-value election machines), Transit/Motor Truck Cargo (for equipment moving between sites), Property in Care Custody and Control (for client equipment at your facility), and Computers/EDP. Endorse blanket waiver of subrogation on IM (Sacramento requirement) and blanket AI/loss payee where required.
discoveryQuestions: What's the replacement cost of your printing presses and sorting equipment? When was the last time those numbers were updated?
When you ship voting machines to a county site, who owns the risk in transit — you or the county? What does the contract say?
Have you ever had a piece of equipment damaged or stolen in transit, and how did that loss play out?
Election cycles drive your revenue — what's your business income exposure if the AZ facility had a fire 30 days before a major election?

findings.contract_quote: (No specific EPLI requirement in either contract; flagged as program completeness gap given client profile.)
findings.policy_quote: No EPLI policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has 50–200 employees and is PE-backed. EPLI exposure (wrongful termination, discrimination, harassment, retaliation, wage & hour defense) is a near-certainty over any 5-year period at this size. PE-backed companies face heightened scrutiny on workforce reductions and culture issues. Election season hiring of seasonal workers compounds exposure. No EPLI was provided in the program submission.
findings.plain_english: At 50–200 employees, statistically you'll see at least one harassment, discrimination, or wrongful-termination claim per year. The average EEOC charge cost is $50K+ even when the company prevails (just defense), and settled cases routinely hit six figures. With PE backing, plaintiffs' attorneys see deeper pockets and run harder. Without EPLI, every defense dollar is paid out of operating cash.
findings.recommendation: Place EPLI at $1M–$3M with: third-party coverage (for non-employee harassment claims by counties' staff/voters), wage & hour defense costs (sublimited is acceptable), broad definition of 'employee' including temps and election-season seasonal hires, and prior-acts retro. Consider full Management Liability package (D&O + EPLI + Fiduciary + Crime) given PE backing.
discoveryQuestions: When you scale up for election season, what's your hiring spike — and what's your training cadence on harassment and wage-hour issues?
Has your PE sponsor required EPLI as part of their portfolio insurance program? Most do.
If a seasonal hire alleged the night supervisor was harassing them, what's the response and who's paying for the lawyer?
How are you currently classifying election-season hires — W-2, 1099, temp agency? That answer drives EPLI definition needs.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Directors & Officers / Management Liability
findings.contract_quote: (No specific D&O requirement in either contract; flagged as program completeness gap given PE-backed status.)
findings.policy_quote: No D&O / Management Liability policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is PE-backed, indicating an institutional sponsor with board representation. D&O personal liability for board members is industry standard for any PE-backed portfolio company. Election services is also a high-attention public-policy industry — boards face derivative claims, regulatory inquiries (DOJ election interference, DHS/CISA), and media-driven litigation. Absence of D&O leaves directors and officers personally exposed and likely violates the PE sponsor's portfolio insurance requirements.
findings.plain_english: Your PE sponsor has board members sitting on Run-Test's board, and they personally have skin in the game on every decision. If a regulator, shareholder, or competitor sues the directors individually — for breach of fiduciary duty, regulatory missteps, or public statements about election integrity — there's currently no policy to defend or indemnify them. PE sponsors typically mandate D&O as a portfolio requirement, so this may already be a covenant breach.
findings.recommendation: Place a Management Liability package (D&O + EPLI + Fiduciary + Crime) at minimum $3M–$5M each. Confirm: full Side A / B / C coverage; entity coverage for securities-style claims; broad definition of 'Claim'; regulatory investigation coverage (formal AND informal); broad insured-vs-insured exception (allowing coverage when investor-insureds sue); prior-pending litigation date appropriate; no PE-style 'bump-up' exclusion; no manufacturing/professional services exclusion barring core operations. Coordinate with PE sponsor's preferred D&O markets.
discoveryQuestions: Does your PE sponsor's investment agreement require you to maintain D&O? Most LPAs and shareholder agreements do.
If a county audit or DOJ inquiry named your CEO or CFO personally, who pays for their lawyer — them, the company, or insurance?
Election integrity is a politically charged area. Have your directors discussed personal liability exposure for public statements or vendor decisions?
When was the last formal indemnification agreement update for your board members? D&O fills the gap when corporate indemnification is unavailable.

findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000. Hired auto liability included (cost-of-hire basis). Non-owned auto liability included (55 employees).
findings.gap_description: Auto policy provides $1M CSL covering owned, hired, and non-owned autos — meets Sacramento's $1M CSL minimum.
findings.plain_english: Auto coverage for Sacramento is right at the line. You meet the contract minimum for owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles.
findings.recommendation: No action required for Sacramento Auto. Note: the same $1M does NOT meet Maricopa's $2M Auto requirement — see separate finding.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Liability Limits — Maricopa County Shortfall
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services or use or maintenance of the premises under this contract.
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M Auto CSL. Auto policy provides $1M CSL — a $1M shortfall on the underlying. Whether this can be cured by an umbrella is interpretively ambiguous (see separate Needs Review finding) — Maricopa §8.2.11 (Auto) does NOT inline-mention umbrella attachment, while §8.2.9 (program-level) permits umbrella stacking generally.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M of Auto coverage. You have $1M. Whether your umbrella (when placed) cures this gap is contractually unclear — the Auto-specific clause doesn't say umbrella can stack, even though the general clause does. The safest read is to either raise primary Auto to $2M or get explicit written confirmation from Maricopa that umbrella stacking is acceptable for Auto.
findings.recommendation: Either: (a) increase Auto CSL to $2M at next renewal (cost is typically modest given fleet of 2 vehicles), OR (b) place an umbrella with explicit Auto follow-form attachment AND obtain written confirmation from Maricopa Risk Management that umbrella satisfies §8.2.11. The cleanest path is option (a) — eliminates contract ambiguity. See Needs Review finding on umbrella interpretation.
discoveryQuestions: What's your reaction if Maricopa rejects an umbrella as a cure for the Auto $2M minimum? Have you seen a county take that position?
Your fleet is two vehicles — the cost differential between $1M and $2M Auto CSL is usually under $1,500/year. Worth eliminating the contract risk?
Have you ever had Maricopa Risk Management push back on a COI before? What's their tendency?

findings.requirement_type: Auto Limit — Maricopa Umbrella Attachment Ambiguity
findings.contract_quote: §8.2.9: 'If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements... the Certificate of Insurance shall indicate which lines the Commercial Umbrella Insurance covers.' // §8.2.11 (Auto): 'Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit... not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence...' (no inline umbrella reference)
findings.policy_quote: Auto $1M CSL underlying. No umbrella in program.
findings.gap_description: Strict reading of Maricopa §8.2.11: Auto must be $2M underlying because the Auto clause does not inline-mention umbrella attachment (compare §8.2.10 CGL which DOES inline-mention umbrella stacking). Permissive reading: §8.2.9 permits umbrella stacking program-wide; $1M Auto + adequate umbrella = compliance. Both readings are tenable. Risk Manager interpretation varies by county and audit reviewer.
findings.plain_english: There's an interpretive question with Maricopa: does umbrella satisfy the $2M Auto minimum, or does Auto need $2M underlying? The contract is genuinely ambiguous. We can't decide this without confirming with Maricopa Risk Management directly.
findings.recommendation: Submit a written interpretation request to Maricopa County Risk Management asking whether umbrella attachment satisfies §8.2.11 Auto. Pending response: defensive posture is to raise Auto primary to $2M. Document the interpretation in the file for future renewals/audits.

findings.contract_quote: The COUNTY... are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects... automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR. (Sacramento §VII.A) // The insurance policies required by this contract... shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds. (Maricopa §8.2.7)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento Pg 3 of 4 §VII.A; Maricopa Pg 5 of 41 §8.2.7
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0478 12 12 — Blanket Additional Insured - Primary and Non-Contributory: 'Any person or organization required by written contract, written agreement or written permit executed before the accident... primary and non-contributory; AI limit is lesser of contract-required or policy limit.'
findings.gap_description: Blanket Additional Insured endorsement (461-0478) extends AI status to any person or organization required by written contract, with primary & non-contributory built in. Satisfies both Sacramento §VII.A/§VII.C and Maricopa §8.2.7 / §8.2.4 for Auto.
findings.plain_english: Both counties get automatic Additional Insured status on your Auto policy by virtue of the contracts they signed with you — with primary coverage that doesn't get reduced by their own insurance. This is correctly built into the policy.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Verify on COI issuance that 461-0478 is referenced and AI status flows correctly. Note exception: AI excluded for sole negligence of the AI, for non-owned/non-trailer auto negligence by AI, and where AI is AI under another liability policy.

findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County... (Maricopa §8.2.8)
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0500 11 13 — Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others to Us: 'BLANKET WHERE REQUIRED BY WRITTEN CONTRACT. Applies only to extent subrogation waived prior to accident or loss under contract.' // Reinforced by 461-0155 Item 18: 'Blanket Waiver preserved through insured contract/written agreement/permit prior to accident.'
findings.gap_description: Two reinforcing forms create a robust blanket Waiver of Subrogation for Auto: standalone 461-0500 plus the Broadening Endorsement 461-0155 Item 18. Both Maricopa and Sacramento Auto WoS requirements are satisfied without scheduling.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy automatically waives the carrier's right to come after the counties for losses, anywhere your contracts require it. Belt-and-suspenders — there are two endorsements doing the same job. Strong.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. (Sacramento §III.B) // ...owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services... (Maricopa §8.2.11)
findings.policy_quote: Item Four — Hired auto liability rated on cost-of-hire basis (AZ class 6611, 'if any' cost of hire). Item Five — Employer's non-ownership liability rated on 55 employees (AZ class 6602).
findings.gap_description: Hired and non-owned auto liability is properly built into the policy with both class codes scheduled. Employee count rated at 55 for non-ownership.
findings.plain_english: When your employees rent a car for a job site, or use their personal vehicles for company errands, your policy responds. Both counties require this, and it's properly in place.
findings.recommendation: Confirm employee count (55) is current — as Run-Test scales (50–200 employees), the rating basis may need updating at renewal or via mid-term endorsement. HNOA premium is exposure-rated.

findings.contract_quote: (General all-policies RMF: knowledge of occurrence should be limited to officer/risk manager.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 17: 'Knowledge of accident requires notice to executive officer/insurance manager.'
findings.gap_description: Knowledge of occurrence properly limited to executive officer / insurance manager — prevents low-level employee's unreported incident from voiding coverage.
findings.plain_english: If a driver has a fender-bender and forgets to tell anyone, that doesn't kill your coverage. The carrier's notice clock only starts when an officer or your insurance contact actually knows about it. Best-in-class language.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Ensure same Notice & Knowledge endorsement is mirrored on every other policy when GL/Cyber/Property/etc. are added to the program.

findings.requirement_type: Auto BI Definition Includes Mental Anguish
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Auto-2: BI definition should include mental anguish standalone.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 21: Mental anguish included in BI.
findings.gap_description: Standard CA 00 01 limits BI to physical injury; the Hanover Broadening Endorsement Item 21 expands BI to include mental anguish as a standalone — closing a common claims gap.
findings.plain_english: If a passenger or pedestrian is mentally traumatized by an auto incident even without obvious physical injury, your policy treats it as covered bodily injury. The broader version of BI is in place.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Unintentional Errors and Omissions Giveback
findings.contract_quote: (RMF General-2: unintentional E&O giveback should be in place.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 19: Unintentional failure to disclose.
findings.gap_description: Hanover Broadening Endorsement Item 19 provides Unintentional Failure to Disclose / E&O giveback — protects against coverage denial for inadvertent failure to disclose a vehicle, location, or operation.
findings.plain_english: If you forget to add a new vehicle or location to the policy and an accident happens, the carrier won't deny coverage just because of the oversight. This is a meaningful protection for a growing fleet/operation.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Replicate this on GL when added.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-4: Lease Gap coverage.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 15: Auto Loan/Lease Gap Coverage.
findings.gap_description: Auto Loan/Lease Gap is included via the Broadening Endorsement — covers difference between actual cash value and loan/lease balance after a total loss.
findings.plain_english: If a financed or leased vehicle is totaled and the bank/lessor wants more than the car was worth, the policy covers the gap. Helpful even for the existing 2-vehicle fleet.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm whether scheduled vehicles are currently financed or leased — coverage is more valuable on financed/leased vehicles.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Named Insureds — Affiliated Entities Scheduled
findings.contract_quote: (RMF General-3: All entities, including LLCs, JVs, holdings, and benefit plans, must be properly named.)
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0174 schedules: Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc, Runbeck Companies 401(k) Profit Sharing Plan, Lincoln Shields LLC, Black Mountain Investment Co. LLC.
findings.gap_description: All affiliated entities — including the LLCs and the 401(k) plan — are explicitly scheduled as Additional Named Insureds via 461-0174. No Broad Form NI endorsement (which often carves out LLCs) is being relied upon — schedule-based naming eliminates LLC carve-out risk.
findings.plain_english: Every Runbeck-affiliated entity I can identify is named on the Auto policy by exact name, not by a broad-form clause that might miss LLCs. This is the safer way to do it.
findings.recommendation: Maintain this approach when GL, WC, Cyber, Umbrella, and Crime are added — schedule each affiliated entity by name on each policy, including the 401(k) plan (especially relevant for fiduciary). Keep the schedule current as the corporate structure evolves.

findings.contract_quote: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. (Sacramento §VI.A.1) // ...AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++. (Maricopa §8.2.1)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento Pg 3 of 4 §VI.A.1; Maricopa Pg 5 of 41 §8.2.1
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Allmerica Financial Benefit Insurance Company (The Hanover Insurance Group). AM Best: A (Excellent), Financial Size XV. Admitted in AZ.
findings.gap_description: Hanover/Allmerica is rated A (Excellent) Class XV by AM Best, exceeding both Sacramento's A-VII threshold and Maricopa's B++ threshold.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto carrier is well above the financial-strength bar both counties set. No issue.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm AM Best rating remains current at each renewal — apply same scrutiny to any added carriers (especially if any GL/Cyber/Crime get placed in the E&S market).

findings.requirement_type: Auto Cancellation Notice — 60-Day For-Cause vs 90-Day Broker Target
findings.contract_quote: (RMF General-1: 90-day notice of cancellation is broker benchmark; less than 60 days is flagged.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 1 (Cancellation Extension): replaces 30-day with 60-day for Auto. Designated Entity NOC 401-1235: 30-day written notice (informational only — does not grant rights). Nonpayment: 10 days.
findings.policy_page: Hanover Auto Pg 48 (461-0155); Pg 44–46 (401-1235); Pg 55 (IL 00 17 baseline)
findings.gap_description: Auto cancellation notice is 60 days for-cause via the Broadening Endorsement — meets Maricopa §8.2.15 (30 days) and exceeds Sacramento's contract-level Contractor notice obligations. However, the broker benchmark is 90 days, and the Designated Entity NOC also stands at 30 days. Compliant with contract minimums but below best-in-class.
findings.plain_english: If your carrier decides to cancel your Auto policy, you get 60 days' notice instead of the standard 30 — which is good, but 90 days is the gold standard. With multi-state county work and a 4-month renewal cycle being typical, more runway helps you avoid coverage gaps that could trigger material breach under both contracts.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate at renewal for a 90-day cancellation extension (some carriers will offer for an additional small premium or no charge). At a minimum, replicate the 60-day language across every policy as the program is built out (GL, WC, Cyber, Umbrella) so notice periods are uniform across the program.
discoveryQuestions: If your Auto policy got cancelled mid-term, how long would you actually need to find replacement coverage and rework all your county COIs? 30 days, 60 days, 90 days?
Have you ever had a carrier non-renew with short notice, and what was the scramble?
Both counties treat lapse as material breach — is 60 days enough cushion if Hanover ever decided to non-renew?

findings.requirement_type: Auto Designated Entity NOC — Maricopa 30-Day Compliance
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. (Maricopa §8.2.15)
findings.policy_quote: Form 401-1235 12 14 — Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): 30-day written notice (other than non-payment). BLANKET WHERE REQUIRED BY WRITTEN CONTRACT plus scheduled entities (City of Boulder, Coconino County, Amazon.com, El Paso County, San Luis Obispo County, State of Colorado, NY State OGS).
findings.gap_description: 401-1235 provides direct 30-day cancellation notice to designated entities including a BLANKET 'where required by written contract' provision. Maricopa is automatically captured. Sacramento is also captured by the blanket provision (no scheduled listing needed).
findings.plain_english: If your Auto policy gets cancelled, the carrier directly notifies any county that has a contract requiring it — automatically. Both Maricopa and Sacramento are covered.
findings.recommendation: No action required. As GL/WC/Cyber/Umbrella are added, ensure each policy has a comparable Designated Entity NOC endorsement with BLANKET 'where required by written contract' wording.

findings.requirement_type: Auto Pollution Coverage — Limited Pollution Endorsement (CA 99 48)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-8: Auto policy should at minimum include the limited pollution endorsement CA 99 48.)
findings.policy_quote: Auto base form CA 00 01 03 06 contains the standard pollution exclusion with carve-back ONLY for fuels/lubricants/exhaust gases needed for normal vehicle operation, and for accidents away from owned/rented premises caused by upset/overturn of a covered auto. CA 99 48 (Pollution Liability — Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos) is NOT in the endorsement schedule.
findings.policy_page: Hanover Auto Pg 33 (base CA 00 01 pollution); endorsement schedule does not list CA 99 48
findings.gap_description: Limited Pollution Liability Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos (CA 99 48) appears to be absent. The base CA 00 01 carve-back covers fuel/exhaust spills from normal operations and overturned-auto pollution events away from premises, but does not cover broader pollution scenarios such as cargo-related fluid releases or environmental damage from auto operation tied to delivery operations.
findings.plain_english: If a delivery vehicle has a serious accident and spills its cargo (ink, toner, batteries from voting machines, hydraulic fluid from equipment), the cleanup costs may not be covered by your Auto policy. CA 99 48 is a small endorsement that fills this gap and is widely available.
findings.recommendation: Add CA 99 48 — Pollution Liability Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos — at next renewal or via mid-term endorsement. Premium impact typically minimal. Separately, consider standalone Contractors Pollution Liability if Run-Test handles ink, toner, batteries, or any chemicals during election machine refurbishment.
discoveryQuestions: Do your delivery vehicles ever transport printer ink, toner, batteries, or any fluids that would create a cleanup obligation if spilled?
If a vehicle accident dumped equipment cargo into a waterway or onto a county property, who pays for the cleanup?
Has any client ever asked about your environmental coverage on the auto side?

findings.contract_quote: (N/A — operational/HR control issue; flagged because exclusion is a coverage trap.)
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0425 (9/10) — Arizona Exclusion of Named Driver: 'Excludes coverage for any accident or loss resulting from operation/use of any covered auto by Malina Trujillo (with exception of UM/UIM).'
findings.gap_description: Named Driver Exclusion bars Liability AND Physical Damage coverage if Malina Trujillo operates any covered auto. UM/UIM still applies. This is an HR/operational control issue — if she or any third party hands her keys, all coverage evaporates for that incident.
findings.plain_english: There's a person specifically excluded from driving company vehicles. If she ever ends up behind the wheel — even one time, even by mistake — your Auto coverage simply doesn't apply to whatever happens. You need a hard control to ensure this never happens.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Malina Trujillo's current relationship to the company (employee, former employee, family member of officer?). Implement (or document existing) HR controls preventing her from operating company vehicles. If she is no longer affiliated with Run-Test, request the exclusion be removed at renewal. If she is still affiliated, document the rationale and circulate to all fleet supervisors.
discoveryQuestions: Who is Malina Trujillo and what's her current relationship to the company? Is the exclusion still relevant?
What controls do you have in place ensuring she never operates a company vehicle, even occasionally?
Has there ever been a near-miss where she could have driven a company vehicle?

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-16: Symbol 1 (any auto) preferred over Symbol 7 (specifically described). Symbols 2/8/9 not equivalent to Symbol 1.)
findings.policy_quote: Policy uses CA 00 01 03 06 base form. Per available analysis: 2 specifically scheduled vehicles (Item Three — symbol 7 implied), Item Four hired auto (symbol 8), Item Five non-owned (symbol 9). Specific Liability symbol selection per Dec page not visible in available extract.
findings.gap_description: Symbol selection on the Liability dec line cannot be confirmed from available data. With only 2 scheduled vehicles, there's a real possibility coverage is on Symbol 7 (specifically described autos) rather than Symbol 1 (any auto). Symbol 7 means coverage applies ONLY to the listed vehicles — adding a vehicle requires endorsement, and unlisted vehicles get no coverage.
findings.plain_english: There's a question about whether your Auto policy covers ANY vehicle the company uses, or only the two specific vehicles on the schedule. If it's the latter, buying a third vehicle without notifying the carrier means it's uninsured. We need to confirm.
findings.recommendation: Pull the Auto Dec page and confirm the Liability symbol assignment. If Symbol 7 (specifically described autos), upgrade to Symbol 1 (any auto) at renewal — premium impact is typically minimal and eliminates the trap. Symbol 1 paired with Symbol 8/9 for hired/non-owned is the cleanest setup.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-18: Insured must understand UM/UIM elections.)
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0368 07 20 — Arizona UM/UIM Coverage Offer and Selection/Rejection. 'Selection initials/signature appear blank/redacted in available chunks — confirm actual elections.'
findings.gap_description: AZ-mandated UM/UIM offer form was issued but the selection page in available extract appears blank or redacted. UM and UIM are currently bound at $1M each per the Dec — but without the executed selection form, there's a possibility of an AZ-statute compliance question or a future dispute about coverage scope.
findings.plain_english: Arizona law requires you to formally elect or reject UM/UIM coverage in writing. We have the form but not the signature. We should confirm a properly executed election is on file with the carrier — otherwise the policy default could apply, which may differ from what you actually want.
findings.recommendation: Request a copy of the executed 461-0368 from Hanover or producer. Confirm UM/UIM at $1M is intentional and signed. File copy.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-5: Drive Other Car endorsement triggered when exec officers are Named Insureds.)
findings.policy_quote: No individual exec officers listed as Named Insureds. NI list is Runbeck Election Services Inc plus 5 affiliated entities + 1 benefit plan — all corporate.
findings.gap_description: N/A — no individual exec officers are Named Insureds, so DOC endorsement is not applicable.
findings.plain_english: Drive Other Car coverage isn't relevant here because no individual is listed as a Named Insured.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Reassess if any individual is added as a Named Insured (e.g., for personal-vehicle owner-operator arrangements).

findings.requirement_type: Auto Mobile Equipment vs. Auto Definition
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-12: Mobile equipment items subject to motor vehicle law must be scheduled on Auto.)
findings.policy_quote: Item Three schedules: 2013 Mercedes Sprinter; 2018 Chevrolet Express. No mobile equipment items scheduled.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test handles election equipment that may include forklifts, pallet jacks, mailing-line tugs, or other powered industrial equipment used to move ballots/equipment. Whether any item meets the 'auto' definition (subject to motor vehicle law and required to be registered) cannot be determined from available data.
findings.plain_english: If you have any equipment that's licensed/registered for road use (even occasionally), it should be on the Auto policy — and if it's only used on private property, it should be on a different policy. We need to inventory the equipment to confirm placement.
findings.recommendation: Run an equipment inventory: forklifts, mailing-line tugs, scissor lifts, riding pallet jacks, golf-cart-style facility transports. For each, confirm whether it requires road registration or is operated on public roads. Items meeting 'auto' definition must be scheduled on Commercial Auto. Items not meeting it should be on GL Mobile Equipment or Inland Marine Contractors Equipment.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-6: CA 9933 Employees as Insureds and CA 2054 Employee Hired Autos.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 4: 'Employees as Insureds when using non-owned/non-hired autos in business.' Item 2: 'Employee Hired Autos under Symbol 8.' Standalone CA 9933 / CA 2054 NOT in endorsement schedule, but the Broadening Endorsement appears to roll equivalent coverage in.
findings.gap_description: The Broadening Endorsement provides functional equivalent of CA 9933 (Employees as Insureds when using non-owned/non-hired autos for business) and CA 2054 (Employee Hired Autos under Symbol 8). Whether the Broadening language is as broad as the standalone ISO endorsements requires close form-to-form comparison.
findings.plain_english: If an employee rents a car for business or uses their own car for a company errand, they appear to be covered as an insured under your policy. The wording comes from Hanover's broadening endorsement rather than the standard ISO form, so we should compare the two side-by-side to make sure it's just as broad.
findings.recommendation: Have producer/Hanover provide a comparison of 461-0155 Items 2 and 4 against ISO CA 9933 and CA 2054 to confirm equivalent or broader scope. If a gap exists, request the standalone ISO endorsements be added.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-9: Fellow Employee Exclusion deletion analysis — pros/cons must be weighed by insured.)
findings.policy_quote: Base form CA 00 01: 'BI to a fellow employee in the course of employment excluded.' 461-0155 Item 6: 'Amended Fellow Employee Exclusion — does not apply to owned/hired autos on excess basis.'
findings.policy_page: Hanover Auto Pg 34 (base) and Pg 53 (461-0155 Item 6)
findings.gap_description: Fellow Employee Exclusion is partially amended via Item 6 — exclusion is dropped to excess basis for owned/hired autos only. Means primary coverage remains absent for fellow-employee BI claims; WC is the primary backstop.
findings.plain_english: If two of your employees are in a company vehicle and one injures the other in an accident, the Auto policy applies on an excess basis behind Workers' Comp. WC will pay first; Auto would only kick in over WC. If WC isn't in place (which is the current situation — see WC missing finding), this is a more pressing exposure.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether broader deletion is desired — full deletion would convert primary Auto coverage for fellow-employee suits, useful where state WC exclusivity rules don't bar tort actions. For Run-Test's profile (employees riding together to county sites), the current excess basis is reasonable IF WC is in place. With no WC currently, this becomes more urgent.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-17: 'Employee' definition modified to exclude leased workers.)
findings.policy_quote: Base CA 00 01 'Employee' definition not modified by any visible endorsement to exclude leased workers.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's seasonal hiring profile (election cycle) creates the possibility of staffing-agency or PEO arrangements. If leased/temporary workers are in the 'employee' definition without modification, they're subject to the Fellow Employee Exclusion AND their entire workers' comp coverage may flow through staffing agency rather than Run-Test's WC. Need to confirm how Run-Test sources seasonal labor.
findings.plain_english: If you use a staffing agency or PEO for election-season scaling, we need to make sure those workers are properly handled in your Auto policy — both for who's covered as an insured and who's excluded for fellow-employee suits. We also need to coordinate with the staffing agency's WC policy.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Run-Test's labor model: direct W-2, staffing agency, PEO, 1099, or mix. If staffing/PEO is used, request: (1) Auto endorsement modifying 'employee' definition to exclude leased workers; (2) Alternate Employer endorsement on the staffing agency's WC policy listing Run-Test; (3) AI status on staffing agency's GL/Auto/WC.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CA-11: No-fault state operations require optional coverage analysis.)
findings.policy_quote: Auto policy is AZ-rated. Item Three vehicles registered in AZ. No no-fault state coverages visible in endorsement schedule.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test serves 31 states + DC. No-fault states include FL, NY, MI, NJ, PA, KS, KY, ND, MN, MA, HI, UT. If Run-Test vehicles or employees drive into any no-fault state, coverage gaps are possible (no PIP, no first-party medical/wage benefits as required in those states).
findings.plain_english: If your van crosses into Florida or your team rents a car for a New York client visit, those states have specific 'no-fault' insurance requirements that aren't built into your AZ-based Auto policy. We should know which states you're driving in and confirm coverage extends correctly.
findings.recommendation: Map states where Run-Test vehicles or rented vehicles operate. For any no-fault state, request appropriate state-specific endorsements (PIP, no-fault, etc.) be added. Confirm hired auto worldwide / nationwide reach (461-0155 Item 20 provides 30-day worldwide on hired autos — confirm domestic non-AZ is fully covered).

findings.requirement_type: Auto Hired Auto Physical Damage Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: (RMF: hired auto physical damage adequacy.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 11: Hired Auto Physical Damage up to $50,000 per accident plus $1,000/day lessor loss of use up to 7 days.
findings.gap_description: $50K per-accident sublimit on hired auto physical damage is below typical replacement cost for many rental vehicle classes (e.g., a high-end cargo van or specialty rental can exceed $50K). For a fleet that may rent specialty trucks during election season, this sublimit may be insufficient.
findings.plain_english: If you rent a high-end truck for an election delivery and total it, the policy pays up to $50K — anything above that is out of your pocket. For most rentals this is plenty, but for specialty cargo or refrigerated trucks it could be light.
findings.recommendation: Confirm typical rental vehicle classes used by Run-Test. If specialty trucks (cargo vans >$50K, refrigerated, or commercial-grade) are routine, request increased sublimit ($100K or $150K) at renewal. Premium impact small.

findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa §8.1.1, Sacramento — indemnity provisions require contractual liability coverage.)
findings.policy_quote: CA 00 01 03 06 §V.H 'Insured contract' definition includes assumed tort liability — supports contractual liability for indemnity assumed in MSAs.
findings.gap_description: Standard CA 00 01 'insured contract' definition is intact (not amended away by endorsement). Assumed-liability under qualifying contracts is covered.
findings.plain_english: When you sign a contract that says 'we'll cover the county for our work,' your Auto policy backs that promise — for auto-related liability — through the standard 'insured contract' carve-back.
findings.recommendation: No action required. When GL is added, confirm it has an unaltered 'insured contract' definition (no CG 21 39 or CG 24 26 contractual liability limitation).

findings.contract_quote: The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability. (Sacramento §VII.D)
findings.policy_quote: CA 00 01 03 06 contains standard Separation of Insureds condition.
findings.policy_page: Hanover Auto base form (Section IV Conditions)
findings.gap_description: Severability/Separation of Insureds is built into the standard CA 00 01 form. Sacramento §VII.D is satisfied at the form level.
findings.plain_english: If the county is sued and one of your employees is also sued, the policy applies to each of them as if they had separate policies (limits aside). Standard and properly in place.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: Contract-level acknowledgment — not a policy endorsement requirement.
findings.gap_description: California Civil Code §2782(b) limits indemnification of additional insureds for the AI's own active negligence on certain construction-style contracts. The Sacramento clause is a contract-level acknowledgement of CA public policy and does not require a special policy endorsement.
findings.plain_english: California law caps how far you can indemnify a county for its own active wrongdoing. The contract just acknowledges that — no policy change needed.
findings.recommendation: No policy action required. Contract drafting team should be aware of §2782 limits when negotiating future indemnity provisions.

findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — Run-Test is an election services manufacturer, not a construction contractor. No physical construction work performed for counties.
findings.gap_description: N/A — Sacramento §III.A per-project aggregate clause is conditional on contractor being engaged in physical construction. Run-Test does not perform construction.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's per-project aggregate clause is for construction contractors. You're not one, so it doesn't apply.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Run-Test does not perform any construction-style work (e.g., physical installation of polling place infrastructure beyond plug-and-play machine drop-off). If any installation activity occurs, reassess whether per-project aggregate is needed on GL.

findings.requirement_type: Course of Construction (COC) Loss Payee & WoS
findings.contract_quote: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR... 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — Run-Test does not perform construction work; no COC/Builders Risk policy needed.
findings.gap_description: N/A — conditional on COC policy being maintained, which is unlikely for an election services manufacturer.
findings.plain_english: COC is for construction projects. Not applicable.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.contract_quote: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: No Inland Marine policy submitted in this program review (see separate missing-Property/IM finding).
findings.gap_description: Conditional clause — only triggers if Run-Test maintains IM. Given high-value election equipment, in-transit cargo, and customer property in care/custody/control, IM coverage is operationally appropriate. If/when IM is placed, blanket WoS endorsement must be added to satisfy Sacramento §IX. Currently, the IM gap itself is the larger issue.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento says 'if you have Inland Marine, waive subro against us.' You probably should have IM (your business depends on equipment in transit), but you don't currently. Two issues: get the IM policy, and make sure when you do, it has the right waiver.
findings.recommendation: Place an Inland Marine policy as recommended in the missing-coverage finding, and at binding, ensure blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement is included where required by written contract.
discoveryQuestions: When you ship voting equipment to a county for an election, who absorbs the loss if it's stolen from the truck?
What's the typical replacement cost of one rack of voting/scanning equipment in transit?
Does the county-issued contract spell out who carries the in-transit risk?

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody, and Control — Customer Property
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CGL-2: Care Custody and Control — third-party property in CCC of insured.)
findings.policy_quote: Auto CA 00 01 §II.B.6 (Pg 34): excludes property damage to property in insured's care, custody or control or transported by insured. Carve-back for sidetrack agreement only — extremely narrow.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test handles county-owned ballots, voting machines, ballot drop boxes, and election-day equipment in its care. Auto Liability fully excludes damage to such property. Without GL Bailee/CCC coverage, Property In-Transit (Inland Marine), or Bailees Customer Property, all damage to county-owned items in Run-Test's possession is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Counties give you their voting machines and ballots to print, sort, and deliver. If anything happens to that equipment while you have it — fire at your facility, dropping a machine, a ballot truck rolls over — your current Auto policy explicitly does NOT cover their property. You'd be on the hook out-of-pocket.
findings.recommendation: Address through (1) GL Bailee/CCC coverage when GL is placed, AND (2) Inland Marine with explicit Property In Care, Custody and Control + Bailees Customer Property coverage. Ensure adequate sublimits given typical value of county equipment in possession (could run $1M+ at peak election season).
discoveryQuestions: At any given moment, what's the dollar value of county-owned property — ballots, machines, drop boxes — sitting in your facility or on your trucks?
If a county-owned vote tabulator was destroyed in your warehouse, what's the conversation with that county look like?
Have you ever damaged a customer's equipment? How was it resolved, and was insurance involved?
Does your contract with each county specify who insures their property while it's in your possession? Some say the county self-insures; some say you do.

findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit. (Sacramento §X) // Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed for any reason... (Maricopa §8.2.15)
findings.policy_quote: Contractor obligation — operational/process control, not policy-driven.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts require Run-Test to notify the counties of claims/lawsuits and policy changes within tight windows. This is a Run-Test internal control rather than an insurance policy provision. Recommend documenting a process so notice obligations are met.
findings.plain_english: Both counties want fast notice if you get sued or if your insurance changes. This is on you, not your carrier — make sure someone owns the notification calendar.
findings.recommendation: Document an internal process: (1) contracts/legal team logs all incoming claims, (2) within 30 days of claim receipt, written notice to Sacramento; within 10 days of lawsuit service, written notice to Sacramento; (3) within 2 business days of any carrier cancellation/material change notice, written notice to Maricopa. Map distribution lists for each county risk manager. Producer can provide template letters.

findings.contract_quote: The Contractor shall maintain all insurance coverages and limits in place at all times and provide the County with evidence of each policy's renewal ten (10) days in advance of its anniversary date.
findings.policy_quote: Operational — producer/broker function.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires renewal evidence 10 days in advance of anniversary. Operationally, producer should issue renewal COIs to all county certificate holders prior to each policy expiration.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento needs a fresh COI 10 days before each policy renewal date. Easy lift; just needs to be on a producer calendar.
findings.recommendation: Establish standing renewal COI distribution: 15+ days before each policy anniversary, broker issues updated COIs to all county certificate holders (Maricopa, Sacramento, and any others). Include all attached endorsement copies per Sacramento §I requirement.

findings.contract_quote: Prior to contract award, Contractor shall furnish the County with valid and complete Certificates of Insurance, or formal endorsements as required by the contract... If a policy does expire during the life of the Contract, a renewal certificate must be sent to County 15 calendar days prior to the expiration date.
findings.policy_quote: Operational — producer/broker function.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires COI naming Maricopa County c/o Risk Management at the specified address and renewal COI 15 days prior to expiration. For claims-made policies, evidence of coverage must extend 2 years past completion.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants COIs delivered to a specific address with renewals 15 days before expiration. Standard producer cadence.
findings.recommendation: Add Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003 to producer's standing certificate-holder distribution. Calendar 15-day renewal COI delivery. For any claims-made coverage placed (Cyber, E&O), maintain 2-year tail or continuous coverage.

findings.contract_quote: Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY. (Sacramento §IV) // The insurance policies may provide coverage that contains deductibles or self-insured retentions. Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. (Maricopa §8.2.6)
findings.policy_quote: Comprehensive deductible: $1,000. Collision deductible: $1,000. No SIR.
findings.gap_description: Auto deductibles ($1,000 each for comp/collision) are routine and disclosable. Maricopa §8.2.6 reserves the right to require bond/LOC for deductibles/SIRs but $1K Auto deductibles are unlikely to trigger that scrutiny. Current setup is benign.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto deductibles are $1,000 each for comprehensive and collision — small, routine, not a concern. When other policies are placed (cyber, E&O, GL), some may have larger SIRs that need to be disclosed and possibly bonded.
findings.recommendation: Disclose all deductibles/SIRs on COIs and in advance to both counties. As cyber and E&O are placed (which often carry $25K-$100K+ retentions), proactively engage Maricopa Risk Management to confirm acceptability and avoid surprise bond/LOC demands.

findings.contract_quote: (RMF UMB-10 by analog: punitive damages exclusion analysis.)
findings.policy_quote: Standard CA 00 01 does not expressly exclude punitive damages. UIM exclusion (461-0680) excludes punitive damages from UIM coverage only. State law in AZ permits insurance for punitive damages in most circumstances.
findings.gap_description: AZ law generally permits insurance of punitive damages. CA 00 01 doesn't expressly exclude them from third-party liability. CA law (where Sacramento sits) prohibits insuring punitive damages directly. For multi-state operations, where punitive coverage applies depends on which state's substantive law governs each claim.
findings.plain_english: If a jury awards punitive damages on top of compensatory damages in an Auto case, AZ law generally lets your insurance cover them — but California law doesn't. For an AZ-based company doing work in CA, this is a state-of-loss question.
findings.recommendation: When umbrella is placed, confirm punitive damages are not excluded (where state law permits). Document that for CA losses, punitives may be uninsurable as a matter of state law (uninsurable, not a policy gap).

findings.contract_quote: (RMF CGL-32 by analog: terrorism coverage analysis. Election services is target-rich infrastructure.)
findings.policy_quote: Form CA 23 85 01 06 — Exclusion of Terrorism Involving Nuclear, Biological or Chemical Terrorism: '(1) dispersal/application of radioactive material or use of nuclear weapon/device; (2) release of radioactive material where terrorism intended such release; (3) dispersal/application of pathogenic or poisonous biological/chemical materials; (4) release of biological/chemical materials where terrorism intended such release.' Conventional terrorism NOT excluded.
findings.gap_description: Conventional terrorism is covered (TRIA does not apply to commercial auto under federal program, but ISO Auto base form does not exclude conventional terrorism without specific endorsement). NBC terrorism is excluded. Election infrastructure is a known target for asymmetric and ideological violence.
findings.plain_english: If a politically motivated attack uses a vehicle as a weapon (Charlottesville-style), or if your fleet is damaged in a conventional terrorist event, your Auto policy does respond. If the attack uses radioactive, biological, or chemical materials, it doesn't. Likelihood is low but the political target profile of election services means this isn't zero.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as configured. Confirm at renewal that no broader terrorism exclusion (e.g., Cap on Losses from Certified Acts of Terrorism, conventional terrorism exclusion) is being introduced. When GL/Property/Cyber are added, evaluate full TRIA terrorism coverage acceptance.
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test received any threats — credible or otherwise — given the public-policy nature of election services?
What's your physical security posture at the AZ facility? Cameras, fencing, controlled access?
Has DHS/CISA reached out about election infrastructure security designation? Many in your industry have.

findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: No cyber policy in program — see separate missing-cyber finding.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa specifically requires claims-made retro before contract effective date and 2-year ERP. With no cyber policy in place at all, no retro/ERP can be established. When cyber is placed, this becomes a binding requirement.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires that when you eventually buy cyber, the retro date covers everything back to before the contract started. The longer you wait to buy cyber, the harder it is to negotiate a retro date that captures pre-2021 work. Buy now.
findings.recommendation: When placing cyber, negotiate retro date back to the original Maricopa contract effective date (or earlier — full prior acts is ideal). If unavailable, document the retro date and disclose to Maricopa Risk Management. At any future cyber non-renewal, exercise minimum 2-year ERP.
discoveryQuestions: When did your relationship with Maricopa start? That determines how far back retro needs to go.
Has there been any cyber incident — even minor — in the last 5 years? It affects how brokers position retro/prior acts requests.
Are you already in negotiation for cyber, or is this a fresh placement?

findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR. B. Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. C. If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed, and not replaced with another claims made policy form with a 'Retro Date' prior to the contract effective date, the CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: No E&O policy in program — see separate missing-PL finding.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires E&O retro before contract effective date, evidence maintained 1 year post-completion, and 1-year ERP if cancelled/non-renewed. With no E&O policy, this requirement is unmet on its face.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has the same retro-date concern as Maricopa, but for professional liability rather than cyber. When you place E&O, the retro must reach back to before this contract — and you need to keep the policy alive (or buy a tail) for at least a year after the contract ends.
findings.recommendation: When placing E&O, negotiate retro to before earliest active Sacramento contract; full prior acts preferred. Maintain coverage for 1 year past contract completion or exercise 1-year ERP. Coordinate retro across all claims-made policies (E&O, Cyber, D&O) to a single common date for cleaner administration.
discoveryQuestions: What's the earliest date Run-Test performed any professional services for Sacramento County or any other county? That sets the retro target.
Have you historically carried E&O? If yes, the retro on your existing or recent policy matters — has it ever lapsed?
When this Sacramento contract eventually ends, how will you maintain coverage for the 1-year tail period? Annual policies or a true ERP?

findings.contract_quote: (RMF — coverage territory adequacy.)
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 20: Hired Auto Worldwide (30 days).
findings.gap_description: Hired auto coverage extended to worldwide for trips up to 30 days. Standard CA 00 01 territory is US/territories/Canada — Item 20 broadens for international employee rentals.
findings.plain_english: If an employee rents a car overseas for a short trip, you have 30 days of coverage. Run-Test is US-focused, so this is a comfort feature.
findings.recommendation: No action required. If international travel exceeds 30 days, address through Foreign Liability/Foreign Voluntary Workers' Comp at that point.
